texts.facts: 2. Facts giving rise to the present petition are that on 17/06/2009, a team constituted by the Collector, Indore comprising Food Inspector Vivek Gangrade visited the establishment of the petitioner namely, Raja Namkeen, 18-B, Chandan Nagar, Indore, which was a proprietorship firm. The petitioner produced photocopy of license for the year 2009-10. After giving information in Form No.6 and after disclosing purpose, the Food Inspector purchased samples of packed snacks (namkeen, sev) by paying cost of the same. Following the due process the samples were sealed and sent to the public analyst, who after analysis submitted report which, in original reads thus:- (1) Insects, Moulds, Rodent hair & Excreta = Absent (2) Rancid odour & Rancid taste = Absent (3) Test for starch = Positive (by Iodine test) (4) Test for salt = Positive (by silver Nitrate test) (5) Test for Turmeric = Negative (by Beric acid test) (6) Extraneous colouring matter = Absent (7) Test for Besan = Positive (by Thin layer chromatography) (8) Test for Teora = Negative (by Thin layer chromatography) (9) Value of the Extracted fat- (i) B.R. Reading at 40 C = 61.7 Irfan vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 14 October, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/107824319/ 1 (ii) Baudouin test for sesame oil = Negative Opinion :- and am of the opinion that the declaration regarding the name and complete address of the Manufacturer and the Manufacturing units, Lot/code/Batch Number which is a mark of identification by which the food can be traced in the manufacture and identified in the distribution and also the date, month and year in which the commodity is manufactured, packed or repacked are not given on the label (packet) of sev (Indorilal Namkeen) which is required as per sub-rule (c)(i), (e), (f) and (I) of Rule 32 of the P.F.A. Rules 1955, hence, it is a contravention of the above Rules. Thus the sample is mis- branded under Section 2(ix), (k) of the P.F.A. Act, 1954. However, the sample contains permitted edible substances. The sample was in a condition fit for analysis. 3. After examining the statement of Food Inspector and other witnesses and the documents produced and proved by them, the trial Court as well as appellate Court found the evidence produced by the prosecution reliable and convicted and sentenced the petitioner as stated above.
texts.arguments: 4. Learned counsel representing the petitioner submitted that the appellant was having valid license for manufacturing of snacks like namkeen sev, therefore, he has good case on merit, but he does not want to press the petition on merits. He only wants to make a submission about the sentence. Placing reliance on the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court rendered in Nemi Chand vs. State of Rajasthan reported in LAWS (SC)-2016-3-119 and followed by Single Bench of this Court in CRR No.3324/2019 (Purushottom vs. State of MP) order dated 19/07/2019, he only prayed that the sentence of the petitioner be removed by enhancing fine amount as is done by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the wake of subsequent development in the law. Relevant paras of the judgment passed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Nemi Chand case (supra) reads thus:- "2. Mr. Sushil Kumar Jain, learned senior counsel appearing for the appellant, submits that though the appellant has some prima facie case even on merits, he would be giving up the plea on merits and his only submission is about the sentence which has been imposed by the courts below. He has, in this behalf, argued that there has been an amendment in the Act by the Central Amendment Act 34 of 1976 whereby Section 16A was added and under the said section, only a fine is leviable. He has drawn our attention to the judgment of this Court in "T. Barai V. Henry Ah Hoe and Another" [1983 (1) SCC 177] wherein this Court held that since the amendment was beneficial to the accused persons, it can be applied even with respect to earlier cases as well which are pending in the Court. In the said judgment, the Court held as under :- "22. The prohibition contained in Article 20(1) is that no person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law in force at the time of the commission of the act charged as an offence prohibits nor shall he be subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of the Irfan vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 14 October, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/107824319/ 2 commission of the offence. The rule of beneficial construction requires that even ex post facto law of such a type should be applied to mitigate the rigour of the law. This finds support in the following passage from Craies on Statute Law, 7th Edn., at pp. 388-89: "Every ex post facto law...." said Chase, J., in the American case of Calder v. Bull "must necessarily be retrospective, but every retrospective law is not an ex post facto law. Every law that takes away or impairs rights vested agreeably to existing laws is retrospective, and is generally unjust and may be oppressive; it is a good general rule that a law should have no retrospect, but in cases in which the laws may justly and for the benefit of the community and also of individuals relate to a time antecedent to their commencement: as statutes of oblivion or of pardon. But I do not consider any law ex post facto within the prohibition that mollifies the rigour of the criminal law, but only those that create or aggravate the crime, or increase the punishment or change the rules of evidence Created On Mon Oct 02 03:31:50 IST 2017 R/CR.RA/662/2013 JUDGMENT and apparent difference between making an unlawful act lawful and the making an innocent action criminal and punishing it as a crime." 5. The judgment passed by this Court in Purushottom case is as under:- "8. In view of the citation of Apex Court which squarely covers the present case, it would be in propriety to substitute the sentence of imprisonment and fine with penalty of Rs.50,000/- in respect of offence for misbranding and adulteration.
